overview: Silla began as the smallest of Korea's Three Kingdoms, in the southeast around Gyeongju, and by 676 had brought most of the peninsula under one rule. Its bone-rank aristocracy, gold crowns, Hwarang youth bands and Buddhist temples made a distinctive civilization that lasted nearly a thousand years.

items.text: Gold crowns with tree and antler uprights, hung with jade and gold spangles, from the royal mound tombs of Gyeongju.
Bulguksa temple and the Seokguram grotto, with its granite Buddha facing the sea, were begun; UNESCO listed both in 1995.
Cheomseongdae, a stone tower built in the reign of Queen Seondeok (632 to 647), is among the oldest surviving astronomical observatories in the world.
The bone-rank system fixed a person's rank, office and even the size of their house by birth.
The Hwarang, bands of aristocratic youths, trained in arms, song and Buddhist and Confucian teaching, and led Silla's armies.
Buddhism became the state religion after the martyrdom of Ichadon, and temples rose across the kingdom.
Gyeongju grew into a planned capital of palaces, temples, markets and tiled houses, with the Anapji pleasure pond laid out in 674.
Court culture prized refinement, poetry in the hyangga form and Buddhist devotion.
The Gyeongju Historic Areas were listed by UNESCO.
Unified Silla's administration, Buddhism and script laid the foundations of later Korean culture.

fall.text: The last king, Gyeongsun, surrendered to Goryeo in 935, ending nearly a millennium of Silla rule counted from its traditional founding in 57 BCE.
